h1:
Walking Ratchaburi's Old Town
Along the Mae Klong River
intro: Ratchaburi sits just about 100 km from Bangkok, an hour and a half by car. But the moment you step into the old quarter along the Mae Klong River, the pace slows right down. Century-old shophouses, an old market that has come back to life, riverside temples, and cafes tucked inside former warehouses. This is the walking route we've put together so you can actually do it all in a single day.

blocks.html: Ratchaburi is a town plenty of people drive straight past on their way south without stopping. But once you walk through the old quarter by the Mae Klong River, you'll see there's far more to look at than you'd expect: old shophouses still trading as shops, a market that has done business since your grandparents' day, old temples facing the water, and a new wave of coffee shops bringing the old streets back to life. We've laid this route out as a loop so you don't have to keep backtracking.

blocks.text: Koh Yi Kee Old Market — the heart of the quarter

blocks.html: If you start anywhere, start at the Koh Yi Kee Old Market on Woradet Road, on the market side of the Mae Klong River. The name 'Koh Yi Kee' comes from Teochew Chinese and means 'by the water', which fits exactly, since this was once a row of timber houses pressed right up against the river. It has been a trading street alongside Ratchaburi for generations. These days it turns into an evening walking street lined with food stalls, snacks, old-fashioned sweets, and handmade goods.

blocks.title: Opening hours matter
blocks.html: Koh Yi Kee Old Market only opens Friday to Sunday and public holidays, in the evening from roughly 4 pm to 10 pm. It's busiest from about 7 to 8 pm. Come on a weekday afternoon and the quarter is quiet with nearly everything shut, so plan your day around it before you set off.

blocks.text: The Old Town Ratchaburi — old warehouses turned community space

blocks.html: A few steps from the Koh Yi Kee market is The Old Town Ratchaburi, the new landmark that has breathed life back into the old quarter. It's a cluster of buildings and warehouses over a hundred years old, renovated with the original frames and walls kept intact, now opened up as cafes, restaurants, and shops. The mood is vintage: bare concrete walls, old timber, warm light, and the whole zone is fun to photograph as you wander. It opens daily from late morning, so it's a spot you can visit even on a weekday when the market isn't running yet.

items.name: sao.home.matcha
items.blurb: A matcha shop inside an old building, with rich green-tea drinks. A good place to rest after walking in the heat.

items.name: Khacha Craft Bar
items.blurb: A small drinks bar in the quarter with a raw, old-warehouse feel.

items.name: Odeng Ya
items.blurb: Korean-style snacks: odeng fishcake skewers served in a warm broth.

items.name: Lao Tong Nee
items.blurb: A shop in the quarter that keeps the old Chinese character of the community alive.

blocks.text: Century-old shophouses and the stories along the street

blocks.html: The real charm of Ratchaburi's old town isn't any single check-in spot. It's walking along Woradet Road and the lanes around it, looking at the old shophouses still standing. Some belong to the Crown Property Bureau and keep their original character almost unchanged: timber doors, old shop signs, moulded plasterwork above the windows. Many still trade as pharmacies, gold shops, and grocery stores run for generations. Walk slowly and look up at the upper floors now and then, and you'll catch details that anyone driving past will never see.

items: Woradet Road — the main street of the old quarter, with shophouses lining both sides, running continuously to the market and cafes.
The Mae Klong riverside embankment — there's a walkway along the water with views of the boats and the far bank, breezy and cool in the evening.
The small community lanes — try turning into a side lane and you'll find old timber houses and the real daily life of the neighbourhood.

blocks.html: Ratchaburi's old town has always sat along the river, so its important temples face the water. They're all a short walk from the market quarter.

items.name: Wat Mahathat Worawihan
items.blurb: A royal temple with evidence dating it back to the Dvaravati period. It sits near the centre of town on the west bank of the river. The highlight is the old prang and a rare back-to-back throne hall arrangement you don't often see.

items.name: Wat Sattanat Pariwat Worawihan
items.blurb: Built in the reign of King Rama V, around 1871, it sits on the bank of the Mae Klong River. The ordination hall is handsome and peaceful, a good place to stop and pay respects while walking along the water.

items.name: Wat Chong Lom
items.blurb: Another riverside temple within the town, near the pumping station, with shady grounds. It's one of the old Mae Klong-side temples the locals hold in high regard.

blocks.title: Dressing for the temples
blocks.html: All three are working temples used by locals. Wear sleeved tops and trousers or skirts that cover the knee, take your shoes off before entering the hall, and keep things quiet out of respect for people who've come to make merit.

blocks.text: Cafes on the Mae Klong — watch the river drift by

blocks.html: Ratchaburi is a cafe town Bangkokians love driving out to, especially the spots right on the Mae Klong River where you can sip coffee and watch the water slide slowly past. Several are within walking distance of the old quarter.

items.name: Tara Coffee
items.blurb: At 84 Woradet Road in the middle of the old quarter, an easy walk from the market. Good coffee and a relaxed mood.

items.name: SOP Cafe
items.blurb: A cafe on the Mae Klong River. The standout is the tunnel entrance, which is fun to photograph, and the riverside zone has a good view.

items.name: Thanks Cafe & Bistro
items.blurb: A riverside cafe in town with both an outdoor riverside zone and an air-conditioned room. Good for escaping the afternoon heat.

blocks.html: Coffee around here mostly runs about 60–90 THB a cup, and cake slices about 70–120 THB, no more than a Bangkok cafe, but with a river view and old-town atmosphere thrown in.

blocks.text: The dragon-jar city — the story that makes Ratchaburi, Ratchaburi

blocks.html: Say Ratchaburi and people picture the dragon jars — the brown-glazed water jars with dragon patterns that have been part of the town for nearly a century. It began around 1933 when Chinese craftsmen who'd migrated and settled here found that Ratchaburi's clay resembled the clay of their homeland and was well suited to pottery. They set up jar kilns that grew into the province's signature product. As you walk through town you'll see dragon jars set out as photo-friendly landmarks in several corners.

blocks.title: Want to see a real jar kiln
blocks.html: If you're curious about where the jars come from, there's a learning centre called 'Rueang Khong Ong' (The Story of the Jar) in Don Tako sub-district on Phetkasem Road, telling the story of jar-making from past to present. It's a little outside the old quarter, so you'll need to take a ride out, but if you like crafts it's worth it.

Within the old quarter is the Ratchaburi National Museum, housed in the former provincial hall. The building itself is fine old architecture worth a look. Inside it tells the story of Ratchaburi from the Dvaravati era, its pottery, and the way of life of the Thai Song Dam people and other ethnic groups in the province. Entry is cheap, and it makes a good stop before or after the market to understand the town a little more.

blocks.text: A real half-day on foot — the route we'd take

items.activity: Start at the Ratchaburi National Museum
items.note: Get a feel for the town's history before you set off; the old building photographs well.

items.activity: Walk along the river to Wat Mahathat Worawihan and the riverside temples
items.note: The sun softens, the walk is easy, and the river breeze is cool.

items.activity: Stop at The Old Town Ratchaburi to photograph the old buildings
items.note: Rest over a coffee at sao.home.matcha or Tara Coffee.

items.activity: Head into Koh Yi Kee Old Market as it opens
items.note: Pick a Friday to Sunday; the crowds aren't thick yet and it's an easy walk.

items.activity: Have dinner in the market, then sit and watch the lights on the river
items.note: Plenty of snacks here, so graze slowly as you go.

blocks.text: Getting there and walking it comfortably

items: Private car — from Bangkok take Phetkasem Road, about 100 km, an hour and a half. Park near the old provincial hall or by the market and walk from there.
Van / coach — vans run from the Southern (Sai Tai Mai) terminal to Ratchaburi all day. Get off in town and walk, or take a motorcycle taxi into the old quarter.
Train — the Southern Line passes Ratchaburi station. Get off and take a short ride into town. Good for anyone who enjoys the train atmosphere.
All on foot in the old quarter — the market, cafes, and temples are all within walking distance. Wear comfortable shoes and bring an umbrella or hat for the afternoon sun.

blocks.title: Make the most of your day
blocks.html: If you only have one day, pick a Saturday or Sunday so you get both the old market in the evening and the cafes during the day. If you can stay overnight, the next morning you can carry on to Damnoen Saduak floating market or Suan Phueng, since they're in the same province.

faq.q: What days and hours is Koh Yi Kee Old Market open?
faq.a: It opens only on Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and public holidays, in the evening from roughly 4 pm to 10 pm, busiest from about 7 to 8 pm. On a weekday afternoon nearly everything is shut, so plan your day to line up before you travel.

faq.q: Are The Old Town Ratchaburi and Koh Yi Kee market the same place?
faq.a: They're two separate spots, but right next to each other in the same quarter and walkable between. The Old Town Ratchaburi is a cluster of old buildings and warehouses renovated into cafes and restaurants, open daily from late morning, while Koh Yi Kee market is an evening walking street only on Friday to Sunday.

faq.q: How long does it take to walk Ratchaburi's old town?
faq.a: Taking it easy and including stops at the temples, cafes, and market, it takes about half a day to a full day. Every spot is within walking distance of the others, so there's no need to drive between them.

faq.q: Is Ratchaburi far from Bangkok, and how do you get there?
faq.a: It's about 100 km away, an hour and a half by car on Phetkasem Road, or you can take a van from the Southern (Sai Tai Mai) terminal or the Southern Line train. Get off in town and you can walk straight into the old quarter.

faq.q: Where can you see the Ratchaburi dragon jars?
faq.a: In the old quarter there are dragon jars set out as photo landmarks in several corners. If you want to see the real story of how they're made, there's a learning centre called 'Rueang Khong Ong' (The Story of the Jar) in Don Tako sub-district on Phetkasem Road, just outside the old quarter.
